lessons.title: Know Your Hot Buttons
lessons.summary: Some topics light you up fast. Knowing them helps.

steps.title: Everyone has hot buttons
steps.body: A certain tone, being interrupted, or comments about money or family can set us off quickly. Knowing your own hot buttons means you can catch the spark before it spreads.

steps.prompt: You notice you always snap when someone comments on your cooking. What’s most helpful?

options.text: Tell people never to mention your cooking again.
options.why: Banning the topic avoids it but doesn’t help you handle the feeling.

options.text: Notice the spark and take a breath before replying.
options.why: Spotting your hot button gives you a moment to choose a calmer reply.

options.text: Snap first; they should know it bothers you.
options.why: Expecting people to guess your triggers often ends in arguments.

steps.prompt: Common hot button, or usually calm topic?

cards.text: Feeling criticised in front of others

steps.why: Hot buttons often touch on respect, fairness or feeling heard. Knowing yours helps you prepare.

steps.prompt: What’s your biggest hot button?
steps.reply: Knowing it gives you power. Next time it’s pressed, you’ll recognise the spark sooner.

steps.body: Write down your top two hot buttons. When one gets pressed this week, take a breath before you reply.

lessons.title: Hungry, Tired, Rushed
lessons.summary: Many arguments start when we’re running on empty.

steps.title: Low fuel, short fuse
steps.body: Hunger, tiredness and rushing make us far more likely to snap. Lots of arguments aren’t really about the topic. They’re about the state we were in when it came up.

steps.title: A tense evening

lines.text: Did you remember to book the dentist? 🦷

steps.prompt: You’re starving and exhausted. What do you reply?

options.text: Can you stop nagging me for once?!
options.why: Tiredness turned a simple question into a sharp attack.

options.text: Not yet, sorry! I’m running on empty. Can I do it after dinner?
options.why: Naming how you feel stops a small question from turning into a row.

options.text: Ignore it until you’ve eaten.
options.why: Silence can feel like a snub and leave them guessing.

steps.prompt: Name your state.
steps.after: right now, so can we talk after I’ve eaten?
steps.why: Naming it with a bit of humour explains your mood and buys time for the real conversation.

steps.prompt: When are you most likely to snap?
steps.reply: Good to know. Saving tricky talks for better moments can prevent a lot of arguments.

steps.body: When a tricky topic comes up while you’re hungry or tired, ask to talk about it once you’ve eaten or rested.

lessons.title: Spot Their Triggers
lessons.summary: Knowing what sets them off helps you avoid needless sparks.

steps.title: Their sparks matter too
steps.body: The people you’re close to have hot buttons too. Learning what upsets them isn’t about walking on eggshells. It’s about choosing your words with care.

steps.prompt: Match their trigger to a gentler approach.

pairs.a: Hates being told what to do

steps.why: Small changes in how you approach things can prevent sparks, without either of you hiding who you are.

steps.prompt: Your dad bristles whenever you give him advice about his health. What’s a better approach?

options.text: Keep giving advice until he listens.
options.why: Pushing on a known trigger usually leads to the same argument again.

options.text: Stop caring about his health.
options.why: Giving up isn’t the only alternative to pushing.

options.text: “How are you feeling about your health lately?”
options.why: A curious question respects him and opens the topic without triggering defences.

steps.prompt: Do you know the hot buttons of the people closest to you?
steps.reply: Learning them, perhaps by simply asking, can make your conversations much calmer.

steps.body: Ask someone close: “Is there anything I say or do that really winds you up?” Listen with curiosity.

lessons.title: Start Gently
lessons.summary: How a disagreement begins often decides how it ends.

steps.title: A soft start
steps.body: Starting a disagreement with blame or sarcasm makes people defensive straight away. Starting with calm words and a focus on the problem gives you a real chance to solve it.

steps.prompt: Soft start, or harsh start?
steps.why: Soft starts invite teamwork. Harsh starts put people on the defensive before the real problem is even discussed.

steps.prompt: Your flatmate keeps leaving dishes in the sink. Which is the gentlest way to start?

options.text: “Are you ever going to wash up?”
options.why: Sarcasm puts them on the back foot immediately.

options.text: “Could we chat about the dishes? It’s been bugging me a bit.”
options.why: Calm and honest, it names the issue without attacking them.

options.text: Pile the dishes on their bed.
options.why: A silent protest can feel hostile and escalate things.

steps.prompt: How do your disagreements usually start?
steps.reply: Knowing your usual start gives you a chance to try a softer one next time.

steps.body: Next time you need to raise a problem, start with “Can we talk about…?” and a calm tone.

lessons.title: Complain, Don’t Criticise
lessons.summary: Talk about the problem, not what’s wrong with them.

steps.title: Complaint vs criticism
steps.body: A complaint is about a specific event: “You didn’t call when you said.” Criticism is about the person: “You’re so unreliable.” Complaints can be solved; criticism wounds.

steps.prompt: Match each criticism to a fair complaint.

pairs.b: “You didn’t ask before taking the car.”
“You were on your phone when I talked.”
“The bill was paid late this month.”

steps.why: Complaints describe what happened, so they can be fixed. Criticism attacks who someone is, which makes them defensive.

steps.prompt: Turn criticism into a complaint.
steps.why: Naming the specific action keeps it fair and gives them something they can change.

steps.prompt: Your partner forgot your anniversary dinner booking. Which is a fair complaint?

options.text: “You clearly don’t care about us.”
options.why: This turns one mistake into a judgement about their feelings.

options.text: “You’re useless at remembering anything.”
options.why: A sweeping insult makes them defend themselves rather than fix things.

options.text: “I was really disappointed the booking was forgotten.”
options.why: It names the event and your feeling, so you can talk about putting it right.

steps.body: Next time you’re annoyed with someone, describe the specific thing they did instead of what you think they are.

lessons.title: Ask for What You Want
lessons.summary: End a complaint with a clear, positive request.

steps.title: Point to the solution
steps.body: It’s easy to say what’s wrong and stop there. Adding what you’d like instead, such as “Could you text if you’ll be late?”, turns a complaint into a path forward.

steps.title: Late again

lines.text: Sorry I’m late, traffic was mad 🚗

steps.prompt: You waited 40 minutes. What do you say?

options.text: It’s fine.
options.why: Hiding your feelings means nothing changes next time.

options.text: You’re always late. It’s so disrespectful.
options.why: Criticism makes them defensive instead of helping fix it.

options.text: I did wait a while. Next time could you text when you’re running late?
options.why: Honest about the impact, with a clear, easy request for next time.

steps.prompt: Add the positive request.
steps.before: It upset me when plans changed last minute.
words: Next time, could we decide together?
steps.answer: Next time, could we decide together?
steps.why: A clear request shows what would help, turning the complaint into teamwork.

steps.prompt: Do you usually say what you’d like instead?
steps.reply: Adding one clear request is a small habit that makes a big difference.

steps.body: When you next raise a problem, finish with “Next time, could you…?” and a specific request.

lessons.title: Stick to One Topic
lessons.summary: Piling on issues turns a small disagreement into a big fight.

steps.title: The kitchen-sink fight
steps.body: An argument about the dishes can quickly become about holidays, in-laws and money. Throwing everything in makes it impossible to solve anything. Keep to one topic.

steps.prompt: You’re discussing who does the school run, and you feel like bringing up their messy desk. What’s best?

options.text: Mention it now while you’re already talking.
options.why: Adding a new issue mid-argument makes both harder to solve.

options.text: Stay on the school run and save the desk for another time.
options.why: One topic at a time means you can actually reach an agreement.

options.text: List every other thing that bothers you too.
options.why: A long list turns a practical chat into a character trial.

steps.prompt: On topic, or kitchen-sinking?

cards.text: “And you forgot my birthday last year!”
“And while we’re at it, your mum…”

steps.why: Staying on topic keeps things solvable. Every added issue makes the argument bigger and harder to finish.

steps.prompt: Do your arguments tend to snowball?
steps.reply: If they do, gently saying “Let’s stick to this one thing” can stop the snowball.

steps.body: In your next disagreement, if new topics creep in, say “Let’s sort this one first.”

lessons.title: Leave the Past Out
lessons.summary: Old hurts brought into new arguments rarely help.

steps.title: Today’s issue, today
steps.body: “You did this last Christmas too!” can feel justified, but dragging up the past usually makes people defensive. Focus on what’s happening now.

steps.prompt: Match the past-digging line to a present-focused one.
steps.why: Present-focused lines keep things fair and solvable. Past-digging makes it feel like a list of charges.

steps.title: An old wound comes up

lines.text: Sorry I couldn’t make your party tonight 😞
Work stuff came up at the last minute.

steps.prompt: You’re disappointed. What do you reply?

options.text: Just like my wedding, when you left early.
options.why: Bringing up old hurts turns one missed party into a long history.

options.text: I was sad you couldn’t come. Can we catch up this weekend?
options.reaction: Yes, I’d love that. Sorry again 💛
options.why: You stayed in the present and kept the door open to reconnect.

options.text: Whatever, not like you care.
options.why: An unfair verdict makes it harder for her to make amends.

steps.prompt: Which old hurt do you tend to bring up?
steps.reply: If one keeps coming back, it may need its own calm talk, separate from today’s issues.

steps.body: In your next disagreement, notice if you’re about to mention the past, and bring it back to today instead.

lessons.title: Name the Real Issue
lessons.summary: The argument about socks might really be about feeling unseen.

steps.title: Look beneath the surface
steps.body: Arguments about chores, phones or plans are often about something deeper: feeling unappreciated, lonely or unheard. Naming that real issue can end a repeating fight.

steps.prompt: Match the surface fight to what it might really be about.
steps.why: When you address the deeper need, the surface fights often fade on their own.

steps.prompt: You keep arguing with your partner about them working late. What might help most?

options.text: “I think I’m really missing time with you.”
options.why: Naming the deeper feeling invites them to help solve it together.

options.text: “Your job is ruining us.”
options.why: Blaming the job makes them defend it instead of hearing your need.

options.text: Keep arguing about the hours.
options.why: The surface fight will repeat until the real need is named.

steps.prompt: Name the real issue.
steps.before: I don’t think it’s really about the dishes.
steps.why: Naming the feeling underneath gets to what really needs fixing.

steps.body: Think of an argument that keeps repeating. Ask yourself: what’s it really about for me?

lessons.title: Call a Time-out
lessons.summary: When it gets too heated, pausing is wise, not weak.

steps.title: Flooded brains can’t talk
steps.body: When we’re very angry, our heart races and it gets hard to think clearly. Calling a short time-out lets you both calm down, so you can talk properly later.

steps.prompt: An argument is getting louder and you feel your heart pounding. What’s best?

options.text: Keep going until someone wins.
options.why: Pushing on while flooded usually leads to words you regret.

options.text: “I’m getting too heated. Can we pause for 20 minutes?”
options.why: A named, time-limited pause lets you both calm down safely.

options.text: Walk out without saying anything.
options.why: Leaving without a word can feel like abandonment mid-row.

steps.title: If you ever feel unsafe
steps.body: Time-outs are for ordinary arguments. If anyone becomes threatening, frightening or violent, leave if you can and contact someone you trust or emergency services.

steps.prompt: Call the time-out kindly.
steps.before: I want to sort this out,
steps.after: and come back in half an hour?
steps.why: It shows you still care about solving it, and the pause is a step towards that.

steps.prompt: What tells you an argument is getting too heated?
steps.reply: That’s your signal. When you notice it, it’s time to call a pause.

steps.body: Agree with someone close on a time-out phrase you can both use when arguments get too heated.

lessons.title: Calm Your Body
lessons.summary: A calm body makes it easier to have a calm conversation.

steps.title: Use the pause well
steps.body: A time-out works best when you actually calm down, rather than rehearsing your argument. Slow breathing, a walk or some fresh air help your body reset.

steps.prompt: Calming, or keeps you wound up?

cards.text: A slow walk around the block
Replaying the argument in your head
Breathing slowly for a few minutes
Texting a friend about how awful they are
A glass of water and some fresh air

steps.why: Calming activities help your body settle. Rehearsing or venting keeps the anger fresh.

steps.prompt: Order a simple calming breath.
steps.why: Longer out-breaths help your body switch out of fight mode, so you can think more clearly.

steps.prompt: What helps you calm down fastest?
steps.reply: Great. Make that your go-to during a time-out.

steps.body: Practise the slow breathing pattern for one minute today, so it’s familiar when you need it.

lessons.title: Come Back to It
lessons.summary: A pause only works if you return to finish the talk.

steps.title: Pausing isn’t dodging
steps.body: If a time-out becomes a way to avoid the topic forever, the problem stays unsolved and trust drops. Coming back when you said shows the pause was about care, not escape.

steps.title: After the break

lines.text: Are we going to finish talking about the holiday?

steps.prompt: You’d rather just drop it. What do you say?

options.text: Let’s just forget it.
options.why: Dropping it leaves the issue to come back, often worse.

options.text: Yes, thanks for waiting. Shall we start with what we both want from the trip?
options.reaction: Good idea. I’d love somewhere warm!
options.why: You returned as agreed and opened with something positive and shared.

options.text: Only if you admit you were wrong first.
options.why: Setting conditions restarts the fight instead of solving it.

steps.prompt: Restart gently.
steps.why: A gentle invitation restarts the talk in a better spirit.

steps.prompt: After a time-out, what tends to happen?
steps.reply: Returning with a gentle opener makes it much more likely you’ll actually sort it.

steps.body: If you pause a disagreement this week, return to it at the agreed time with a gentle opening line.

lessons.title: Repeat Their View
lessons.summary: Say their side back before you argue yours.

steps.title: Show you heard
steps.body: Before making your point, try repeating theirs: “So you feel I made the decision without you?” It shows you’re listening and often calms things instantly.

steps.prompt: Your friend says, “You always pick where we go.” What’s the best first response?

options.text: “That’s not true, you chose last time!”
options.why: Jumping to defend yourself skips over how they feel.

options.text: “So it feels like your choices don’t count much?”
options.why: Reflecting their view shows you heard them before you explain your side.

options.text: “Fine, you choose everything from now on.”
options.why: A sulky reply shuts down the conversation instead of understanding it.

steps.prompt: Reflect their view.
steps.before: So what I’m hearing is that you feel
steps.why: Naming their feeling shows you’re trying to understand, not to win.

steps.prompt: Put these steps for disagreeing well in order.
steps.why: When people feel heard first, they’re much more ready to hear you.

steps.body: In your next disagreement, repeat the other person’s view back before you share your own.

lessons.title: Find What’s Fair
lessons.summary: Look for the bit of their point that makes sense.

steps.title: Find the grain of truth
steps.body: Even when you disagree, there’s usually something fair in what the other person says. Acknowledging it, “You’re right that I’ve been busy”, lowers defences on both sides.

steps.prompt: Match their complaint to the fair bit you could agree with.

pairs.b: “I have been out a lot lately.”

steps.why: Agreeing with the fair part doesn’t mean agreeing with everything. It shows good faith and calms things down.

steps.prompt: Your mum says, “You never visit any more.” You visit monthly. What’s best?

options.text: “That’s ridiculous, I came last month!”
options.why: Correcting her bluntly ignores the feeling behind her words.

options.text: Say nothing and feel annoyed.
options.why: Staying silent leaves both of you feeling unheard.

options.text: “I know it’s been less than before. Shall we plan some regular visits?”
options.why: You acknowledged what’s fair and offered a positive way forward.

steps.prompt: How easy is it for you to admit someone has a fair point?
steps.reply: It gets easier with practice, and it often softens the whole conversation.

steps.body: In your next disagreement, find one thing the other person said that’s fair, and say so out loud.

lessons.title: Curious, Not Certain
lessons.summary: Ask questions before deciding what they meant.

steps.title: We often guess wrong
steps.body: In a disagreement, we tend to assume we know why the other person did something. Asking “What was going on for you?” often reveals a reason we never expected.

steps.prompt: Curious question, or certain accusation?

cards.text: “I know exactly why you did it.”

steps.why: Curiosity opens the conversation. Certainty closes it, and often turns out to be wrong.

steps.title: A missed call

lines.text: Sorry I didn’t call back yesterday.
It was a bit of a day.

steps.prompt: You’d assumed they were avoiding you. Reply?

options.text: No worries. Is everything okay? Want to talk?
options.reaction: Actually… yeah, my nan’s not well 😔
options.why: Curiosity opened the door to what was really going on.

options.text: I figured you were ignoring me.
options.why: Sharing your assumption made them defend themselves instead of open up.

options.text: Fine.
options.why: A cold reply shuts down any chance of hearing what happened.

steps.prompt: When do you jump to conclusions most?
steps.reply: Knowing that helps. Those are the moments to swap certainty for a question.

steps.body: Next time you feel sure about why someone did something, ask them a curious question instead.

lessons.title: Own Your Part
lessons.summary: Even if it’s only a small part, owning it helps.

steps.title: Find your ten per cent
steps.body: In most disagreements, both people play a part, even if one seems bigger. Owning your piece, “I did raise my voice”, often makes it easier for the other person to own theirs.

steps.prompt: You and your brother had a row about a family plan. You think he was mostly wrong. What helps?

options.text: Wait for him to apologise first.
options.why: Waiting can leave you both stuck, each hoping the other moves.

options.text: Tell him exactly how wrong he was.
options.why: Focusing only on his part makes him defend himself.

options.text: “I could’ve said things more calmly. Can we try again?”
options.why: Owning your small part often invites him to own his too.

steps.prompt: Own your part.
steps.why: Naming one specific thing you did shows honesty and invites repair.

steps.prompt: How easy is it for you to own your part?
steps.reply: That’s honest. Even a small “I could have done better” goes a long way.

steps.body: After your next disagreement, name one thing you could have done differently, and share it with them.

lessons.title: Skip the Excuse
lessons.summary: Explaining why you did it can sound like you don’t mean sorry.

steps.title: Reasons can wait
steps.body: When owning your part, it’s tempting to add why it happened. But reasons straight away can sound like excuses. Own it first; explanations can come later if they’re wanted.

steps.prompt: Owning it, or excusing it?

cards.text: “I snapped at you. That wasn’t fair.”
“I forgot, but you didn’t remind me.”

steps.why: Owning it focuses on the impact on them. Excuses shift the focus to you and your reasons.

steps.prompt: You missed your friend’s big presentation. Which response owns it best?

options.text: “I’m so sorry I missed it. I know how much it mattered.”
options.why: It owns the miss and acknowledges what it meant to them.

options.text: “Sorry, the bus was late and my phone died and…”
options.why: A list of reasons can feel like you’re defending yourself.

options.text: “You’ll have other presentations.”
options.why: Brushing it off makes their disappointment feel unimportant.

steps.prompt: What excuse do you reach for most?
steps.reply: Noticing it is half the battle. Try leaving it out next time.

steps.body: Next time you own a mistake, stop after the apology. Only explain if they ask.

lessons.title: Show You’ve Learned
lessons.summary: Owning your part matters most when you change next time.

steps.title: Change says the most
steps.body: Owning a mistake is powerful, but doing it differently next time is what people remember. Small, visible changes show your apology was real.

steps.prompt: Match the mistake to a visible change.
steps.why: Visible changes show you took the lesson to heart. They rebuild trust more than words alone.

steps.title: A second chance

lines.text: My mum’s invited us for Sunday lunch.
Last time you said yes without checking with me…

steps.prompt: You’ve learned from last time. Reply?

options.text: Let’s check our plans first. Do you want to go?
options.reaction: Thank you for asking 💛 Yes, let’s go!
options.why: You showed the lesson in action by checking with them first.

options.text: I already told her yes, sorry!
options.why: Repeating the same mistake undoes the earlier apology.

options.text: Ugh, do we have to talk about last time?
options.why: Getting defensive misses the chance to show you’ve changed.

steps.prompt: What’s one change you’ve made after a past disagreement?
steps.reply: That’s worth being proud of. Each change makes future disagreements easier.

steps.body: Pick one lesson from a recent disagreement and show it in action this week.

lessons.title: Brainstorm Together
lessons.summary: List ideas together before choosing a solution.

steps.title: More ideas, better fixes
steps.body: When you’re stuck, it helps to list lots of possible solutions together, even silly ones, before picking. It turns a battle into a joint project.

steps.prompt: Put a joint brainstorm in order.
items: Pick a few you both like
steps.why: Agreeing on the problem keeps you aligned. Listing ideas freely before judging helps you find options you both like.

steps.prompt: You disagree about where to spend Christmas. What’s a good brainstorming move?

options.text: “Let’s list every option, even unusual ones, then pick together.”
options.why: Listing freely opens up ideas neither of you had thought of.

options.text: “We’re going to my parents’. That’s final.”
options.why: Deciding alone turns a shared problem into a power struggle.

options.text: “Let’s just not do Christmas.”
options.why: Giving up avoids the conflict but leaves both of you unhappy.

steps.prompt: Invite brainstorming.
steps.before: We both want a fair answer.
words: What ideas can we come up with?
steps.answer: What ideas can we come up with?
steps.why: It invites teamwork and makes the solution something you build together.

steps.body: Next time you’re stuck on a disagreement, write down at least five possible solutions together before choosing.

lessons.title: Try It for a Week
lessons.summary: Treat a solution as an experiment, not a forever rule.

steps.title: Experiments feel easier
steps.body: Agreeing to something forever feels huge. Agreeing to try it for a week feels doable. Afterwards, you can check in and adjust together.

steps.title: Sharing the chores

lines.text: I don’t think a chore rota will work for us.
It’s just going to cause more arguments 😕

steps.prompt: What do you suggest?

options.text: Fine, then you do all the cleaning.
options.why: An ultimatum makes the disagreement bigger, not smaller.

options.text: Forget it then.
options.why: Giving up means the problem stays as it is.

options.text: Shall we try it for just one week, then see how it went?
options.why: A short trial lowers the stakes and makes it easier to say yes.

steps.prompt: Order a trial solution.
items: Set a time to check in
steps.why: A set check-in time makes the trial feel safe. Reviewing together lets you tweak it fairly.

steps.prompt: Which ongoing disagreement could use a trial solution?
steps.reply: Great pick. A one-week experiment there could break the deadlock.

steps.body: Suggest a one-week trial for something you’ve been disagreeing about, and set a time to review it.

lessons.title: Agree to Differ
lessons.summary: Some disagreements don’t need solving. Respect is enough.

steps.title: Not every gap needs closing
steps.body: Some differences, like politics, taste or habits, may never be resolved. That’s okay. Agreeing to differ respectfully can be healthier than fighting the same fight forever.

steps.prompt: Needs solving, or fine to agree to differ?
steps.why: Practical, shared decisions need solving. Matters of taste and opinion can usually live side by side.

steps.prompt: You and your uncle always argue about politics at family dinners. What’s a healthy step?

options.text: Keep debating until one of you changes their mind.
options.why: Deeply held views rarely change over dinner, so it repeats.

options.text: “We see this differently, and that’s okay. How’s the garden?”
options.why: It respects you both and moves the conversation somewhere warmer.

options.text: Stop going to family dinners.
options.why: Avoiding the whole family costs much more than the disagreement.

steps.prompt: Which disagreement could you let rest?
steps.reply: Letting it rest can bring a lot of peace back into that relationship.

steps.body: Think of one difference you keep arguing about. Next time it comes up, try saying, “We see this differently, and that’s okay.”

lessons.title: Reach Out First
lessons.summary: Going first after a fight is strength, not weakness.

steps.title: Someone has to go first
steps.body: After a row, people often wait for the other to make the first move. A simple “I don’t like us being like this” can end a stand-off and start healing.

steps.prompt: You and a friend haven’t spoken for three days since a disagreement. What helps most?

options.text: Wait. They should message first.
options.why: Waiting can stretch the silence into weeks.

options.text: Post something pointed on social media.
options.why: Indirect jabs make the rift bigger and more public.

options.text: “I’ve missed you. Can we talk about the other day?”
options.why: Going first with warmth shows the friendship matters more than being right.

steps.prompt: Reach out warmly.
steps.before: I don’t like us being at odds.
steps.why: A short, warm invitation opens the door without blaming anyone.

steps.prompt: After a disagreement, who usually reaches out first?
steps.reply: Whoever it is, being willing to go first is a real gift to any relationship.

steps.body: If you’re in a stand-off with someone, send a short, warm message to reach out first.

lessons.title: Repair Attempts
lessons.summary: A joke, a touch or a kind word can calm a row midway.

steps.title: Little bids to reconnect
steps.body: During a disagreement, small gestures like a gentle joke, “Can I try again?” or a soft touch are bids to reconnect. Noticing and accepting them can stop a fight spiralling.

steps.prompt: Match the repair attempt to a good way to accept it.

pairs.a: A small joke to ease tension

steps.why: Accepting a repair attempt lowers the temperature for both of you. Rejecting it can make things worse.

steps.title: Mid-argument
steps.prompt: You’re still a bit cross. What do you reply?

options.text: Tea won’t fix this.
options.why: Rejecting the olive branch keeps the argument going.

options.text: Truce. And yes please, two sugars 😅
options.reaction: Coming right up. Let’s talk calmly after?
options.why: Accepting their repair lets you both reset and talk better.

options.text: Ignore the message.
options.why: Silence can feel like a rejected apology.

steps.prompt: What repair attempts do you use?
steps.reply: Knowing your own helps you notice theirs too.

steps.body: In your next disagreement, notice if they try to repair it, and accept the gesture warmly.

lessons.title: Talk About the Fight
lessons.summary: Once calm, chat about what happened and what helped.

steps.title: Learn from the row
steps.body: When things are calm again, a short chat about what happened can stop it repeating. What set it off? What made it worse? What helped? Treat it like a team review, not a trial.

steps.prompt: Order a calm after-fight chat.
items: Agree on one thing to try next time
steps.why: Waiting for calm keeps it kind. Ending with one shared plan makes the next disagreement easier.

steps.prompt: A day after a row about money, you’re both calm. What’s a good way to start the review?

options.text: “Let’s talk about why you were so unreasonable.”
options.why: Starting with blame reopens the fight.

options.text: “Can we chat about yesterday, so it goes better next time?”
options.why: It frames the talk as teamwork for the future.

options.text: Never mention it again.
options.why: Avoiding it means the same row may happen again.

steps.prompt: Focus on next time.
steps.before: Next time, it might help if we
steps.why: A specific, shared idea helps you both handle the next disagreement better.

steps.body: After your next disagreement, once calm, ask: “What could we do differently next time?”

lessons.title: Spot Your Loop
lessons.summary: Many couples and families have the same fight on repeat.

steps.title: The same old dance
steps.body: Often, the same argument plays out in the same way: one person pushes, the other withdraws, round and round. Spotting your loop is the first step to stepping out of it.

steps.prompt: Match the loop to how it keeps going.
steps.why: Each person’s move makes sense, but together they keep the loop spinning. Seeing it makes it easier to change.

steps.prompt: You notice: when you raise money worries, your partner changes the subject, and you push harder. What helps?

options.text: Push even harder so they have to listen.
options.why: Pushing harder usually makes them pull back further.

options.text: “I think we have a pattern. Can we look at it together?”
options.why: Naming the loop as a shared problem helps you both step out of it.

options.text: Stop raising money altogether.
options.why: Avoiding the topic leaves the worry unsolved.

steps.prompt: Which loop shows up most in your relationships?
steps.reply: Even noticing it is a big step. The next lesson looks at changing one move.

steps.body: Think of an argument that repeats. Write down who usually does what, and look for your loop.

lessons.title: Change One Step
lessons.summary: Changing your own move can break the whole loop.

steps.title: You only need to change you
steps.body: You can’t control the other person’s part of the loop. But changing your own move, like asking calmly instead of pushing, often shifts the whole pattern.

steps.prompt: Breaks the loop, or keeps it going?

cards.text: Asking a calm question instead of pushing
Staying in the room instead of walking off

steps.why: A small change in your move gives the other person room to respond differently too.

steps.title: The usual argument

lines.text: I KNOW, I’ll tidy my room later.

steps.prompt: Usually you’d nag more. Try a new move?

options.text: I’ve asked a hundred times!
options.why: The same old move gets the same old response.

options.text: Okay. When would suit you? Before dinner?
options.why: A calm question instead of nagging changed the dance.

options.text: Tidy it yourself and sulk.
options.why: Silent resentment keeps a different version of the loop going.

steps.prompt: What’s one move you could change in your loop?
steps.reply: Brilliant. Try it once and notice what changes.

steps.body: Next time your usual argument starts, change just your own first move and see what happens.

lessons.title: Fight for the Team
lessons.summary: It’s you two against the problem, not against each other.

steps.title: Same side of the table
steps.body: Healthy disagreements feel like two people solving a puzzle together, not two opponents. Reminding yourselves you’re on the same team changes how every argument feels.

steps.prompt: Bring it back to the team.
steps.before: We’re on the same side here.
words: How do we fix this together?
steps.answer: How do we fix this together?
steps.why: It turns the argument into a shared problem you can solve side by side.

steps.prompt: You and your partner disagree about a big purchase. What keeps it a team effort?

options.text: “What matters most to each of us here?”
options.why: It looks for what you both need, so the answer works for the team.

options.text: “I earn more, so I decide.”
options.why: Pulling rank turns a shared decision into a contest.

options.text: Buy it anyway and deal with it later.
options.why: Acting alone damages trust and the sense of being a team.

steps.prompt: Match the opponent line to a team line.
steps.why: Team language reminds you both that the relationship matters more than winning.

steps.prompt: What have you learned most about conflict in these lessons?
steps.reply: Wonderful. Disagreements will still happen, and now you have tools to handle them well.

steps.body: In your next disagreement, say out loud: “We’re on the same team. How do we fix this together?”
